extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and natural philosophers studying classical gravitation (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction and summarization of propositions/theorems from Newton's Principia concerning laws of attraction between bodies (spheres, shells, solids) and how pointwise centripetal force laws integrate to produce total forces. Includes constructive problems and corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXV. Theor. XXXV
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad Sphæræ datæ puncta singula tendant vires æquales centripetæ decrescentes in duplicata ratione distantiarum a punctis, dico quod Sphæra quævis alia similaris attrahitur vi reciproce proportionali quadrato distantiæ centrorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: The attraction of each particle is inverse-square in its distance from the attracting sphere's centre (via prior theorems), so the sphere acts as if all attraction came from a single central particle; by previous results that central-body attraction is inverse-square, the whole sphere's attraction on a similar sphere is inverse-square in the centres' distance. Corollaries: (1) attraction of spheres toward other homogenous spheres is proportional to their contents applied to the square of the distance between centres; (2) the same holds when the attracted sphere also attracts (mutual forces double by Newton's 3rd law); (3–4) analogous results for motion in conic sections when attraction centers are located at the umbilic or when motion occurs inside the sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXVI. Theor. XXXVI
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Sphæræ in progressu a centro ad circumferentiam (quod materiæ densitatem & vim attractivam) utcunq; dissimilares, in progressu vero per circuitum ad datam omnem a centro distantiam sunt undiq; similares, & vis attractiva puncti cujusq; decrescit in duplicata ratione distantiæ corporis attracti: dico quod vis tota qua hujusmodi Sphæra una attrahit aliam sit reciproce proportionalis quadrato distantiæ centrorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that concentric spherical shells (possibly with radially varying density and pointwise attraction) each attract another sphere by inverse-square in centre separation; summing/integrating over shells preserves inverse-square law. Corollaries (1–9) give consequences: mutual attractions of many similar spheres, relations at unequal distances (applied to squares of centre separations), accelerative and ponderous attractions proportional to products of contents, equal periodic times if separations proportional to diameters, and generalizations when attractivity is mutual or spheres are rotating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXVII. Theor. XXXVII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad singula Sphærarum puncta tendant vires centripetæ proportionales distantiis punctorum a corporibus attractis: dico quod vis composita, qua Sphæræ duæ se mutuo trahent, est ut distantia inter centra Sphærarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If at each point of spheres the centripetal force is proportional to the distance from the attracted bodies, then the total mutual attraction between the two spheres is proportional to the distance between their centres. Multiple 'Cases' demonstrate interior/exterior placements: (Case 1) derive by integrating contributions of circular planes; (Cases 2–6) extend to when the attracted point lies inside a sphere or when assembling one sphere from many particles, showing the composite force scales linearly with centre separation and doubling under mutual attraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXVIII. Theor. XXXVIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Sphæræ in progressu a centro ad circumferentiam sint utcunq; dissimilares & inæquabiles, in progressu vero per circuitum ad datam omnem a centro distantiam sint undiq; similares; & vis attractiva puncti cujusq; sit ut distantia corporis attracti: dico quod vis tota qua hujusmodi Sphææ duæ se mutuo trahunt sit proportionalis distantiæ inter centra Sphærarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct corollary of the previous proposition: when pointwise attraction is proportional to distance, the total attraction between such (possibly radially inhomogeneous) spheres is proportional to centre separation. Corollary: previously demonstrated results about conic-section motion apply when attractions are of this form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium (notable cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attractionum Casus duos insigniores jam dedi expositos; nimirum ubi vires centripetæ decrescunt in duplicata distantiarum ratione, vel crescunt in distantiarum ratione simplici; efficientes in utroq; Casu ut corpora gyrentur in Conicis Sectionibus, & componentes corporum Sphæricorum vires centripetas eadem lege in recessu a centro decrescentes vel crescentes cum seipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation that two especially important laws of pointwise centripetal force—(a) inverse-square decrease and (b) direct proportionality to distance—both produce motions in conic sections and other elegant conclusions; other cases are possible but yield less elegant results, motivating a general method to treat them together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXIX
rubrics_metrics.description: If a circle with centre S has two infinitely small arcs EF and ef whose convolutions describe a concavo-convex solid about axis PS, then as the distance between the arcs tends to zero the limiting ratio of the vanishing line Dd to Ff equals PE to PS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometrical limiting lemma used in subsequent integration arguments: relates infinitesimal elements on a surface of revolution to corresponding linear proportions (PE:PS). Proof uses similar triangles and limiting arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXIX. Theor. XXXIX
rubrics_metrics.description: Si superficies ob latitudinem infinite diminutam jamjam evanescens EFfe, convolutione sui circa axem PS, describat solidum Sphæricum concavo-convexum, ad cujus particulas singulas æquales tendant æquales vires centripetæ: dico quod vis, qua solidum illud trahit corpusculum situm in P, est in ratione composita ex ratione solidi DEq. × Ff & ratione vis qua particula data in loco Ff traheret idem corpusculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives how the force of a thin spherical shell (surface of revolution of an infinitesimal arc) on a particle P can be computed: proportional to DE^2 × Ff times the force a particle at location Ff would exert. Proof integrates annular contributions and expresses result via surface element geometry (Archimedean relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXX. Theor. XL
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad Sphæræ alicujus AEB, centro S descriptæ, particulas singulas æquales tendant æquales vires centripetæ, & ad Sphæræ axem AB, in quo corpusculum aliquod P locatur, erigantur de punctis singulis D perpendicula DE, Sphæræ occurrentia in E, & in ipsis capiantur longitudines DN, quæ sint ut quantitas DEq. × PS ÷ PE & vis quam Sphæræ particula sita in axe ad distantiam PE exercet in corpusculum P conjunctim: dico quod vis tota, qua corpusculum P trahitur versus Sphæram, est ut area comprehensa sub axe Sphæræ AB & linea curva ANB, quam punctum N perpetuo tangit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive description: divide sphere into infinitesimal spherical shells and relate their contributions to ordinates DN proportional to DE^2 × PS/PE and the particle's force. Summing gives that the total attraction is proportional to the area under the axis AB bounded by the curve ANB. Corollaries: special cases when particlewise attraction is constant, inverse, inverse-square, inverse-cube, or general V lead to explicit forms for DN and hence for ABNA area representation of total force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXI. Prob. XLI
rubrics_metrics.description: Stantibus jam positis, mensuranda est Area ABNA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: constructively measure the area ABNA described in Prop. LXXX. Method: draw tangent from P, erect normal, bisect, and express DE^2/(PE×V) as sum of three parts which resolve into areas under known curves. Examples: (1) particlewise centripetal force inverse to distance: DN yields combination of rectangular, parabolic and hyperbolic areas leading to an explicit geometric construction (hyperbola asymptotes, chords closing area); (2) particlewise inverse-cube: analogous decomposition with hyperbolic and rectangular components; (3) inverse-quartic example yields eventual result that total force on central particle is ∝ SI^3 / PI (i.e., inverse-cubic product). The proposition provides explicit geometric quadratures to obtain the required area and thus total force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXII. Theor. XLI
rubrics_metrics.description: In Sphæra centro S intervallo SA descripta, si capiantur SI, SA, SP continue proportionales: dico quod corpusculi intra Sphæram in loco quovis I attractio est ad attractionem ipsius extra Sphæram in loco P, in ratione composita ex dimidiata ratione distantiarum a centro IS, PS & dimidiata ratione virium centripetarum, in locis illis P & I, ad centrum tendentium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a relation comparing attraction experienced by a particle inside the sphere at I to that experienced outside at P, when SI, SA, SP are in continued proportion. For pointwise attraction laws following PE^n/IE^n, the ratio of total attractions is composed of half-ratios of distances and half-ratios of pointwise centripetal forces at the two locations. Concrete consequences: for inverse-square point forces the interior attraction equals exterior; for inverse-cube the interior attraction varies as SP^4 relative to SA^4 etc.; shows how interior and exterior attractions transform with power laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXIII. Prob. XLII
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire vim qua corpusculum in centro Sphæræ locatum ad ejus segmentum quodcunq; attrahitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: compute the force that a spherical segment (bounded by a plane) exerts on a particle at the sphere's centre. Method: decompose the spherical segment using a nearby spherical surface of small thickness (physical surface), express its contribution via PF×DF×O (Archimedean result), assume particlewise forces ∝ distance^(-n), and show net force is proportional to DF×O/PF^{n-1}; representable by a perpendicular whose ordinates applied along the segment give a curve whose area equals the total force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXIV. Prob. XLIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire vim qua corpusculum, extra centrum Sphæræ in axe segmenti cujusvis locatum, attrahitur ab eodem segmento.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: compute attraction by a spherical segment on a particle located externally on the segment's axis. Approach: split segment into two parts, compute attraction of each (one via Prop. LXXXI and the other via Prop. LXXXIII), and sum to obtain the total. Scholium notes that similar methods extend to other attracting bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXV. Theor. XLII (Sect. XIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corporis attracti, ubi attrahenti contiguum est, attractio longe fortior sit, quam cum vel minimo intervallo separantur ab invicem: vires particularum trahentis, in recessu corporis attracti, decrescunt in ratione plusquam duplicata distantiarum a particulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that if attraction dramatically increases in contact (much stronger than at small separation), then the pointwise forces composing the attracting body must decrease faster than inverse-square with distance from the attracted body. Argument: inverse-square point law would not produce such a large contact effect; therefore for bodies to show much stronger contact attraction the pointwise law must decay faster than quadratic. Analogous conclusions for spherical and concave bodies are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXVI. Theor. XLIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si particularum, ex quibus corpus attractivum componitur, vires in recessu corporis attracti decrescunt in triplicata vel plusquam triplicata ratione distantiarum a particulis: attractio longe fortior erit in contactu, quam cum attrahens & attractum intervallo vel minimo separantur ab invicem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pointwise forces decrease as inverse-cube or more rapidly, then the attraction in contact becomes arbitrarily large compared with that at small separations — shown by previous Problem XLI examples. Extends to orbs and concentric shells by similar computations; adding/removing matter far from contact does not greatly change the contact effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXVII. Theor. XLIV
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora duo sibi invicem similia & ex materia æqualiter attractiva constantia seorsim attrahant corpuscula sibi ipsis proportionalia & ad se similiter posita: attractiones acceleratrices corpusculorum in corpora tota erunt ut attractiones acceleratrices corpusculorum in eorum particulas totis proportionales & in totis similiter positas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two similar bodies, made of equally attractive material, attract small particles proportional to their masses and similarly placed, then the overall accelerative attractions between the whole bodies are proportional to those between corresponding small parts. Corollaries: this gives scaling laws — if pointwise force decays as D^(-n), then whole-body accelerations scale with body sizes accordingly (examples: n=2 yields accelerations ∝ linear dimensions; n=3 gives equal accelerations regardless of size; n=4 gives accelerations reciprocally proportional to linear dimensions, etc.). Also allows inferring the decay law of pointwise forces from measured whole-body attractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXVIII. Theor. XLV
rubrics_metrics.description: Si particularum æqualium corporis cujuscunq; vires attractivæ sint ut distantiæ locorum a particulis: vis corporis totius tendet ad ipsius centrum gravitatis; & eadem erit cum vi globi ex materia consimili & æquali constantis & centrum habentis in ejus centro gravitatis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a body's equal particles exert attraction proportional to distance, then the total attraction of the body tends to and equals that of its centre of gravity — i.e., the body acts as if all its mass were concentrated at the centre of gravity. Corollary: motion of attracted bodies will be the same as if the attracting body were a sphere concentrated at its CG; hence if the CG is stationary or uniform straight motion, attracted bodies move in ellipses centered on the attracting body's centre of gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXIX. Theor. XLVI
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Corpora sint plura ex particulis æqualibus constantia, quarum vires sunt ut distantiæ locorum a singulis: vis ex omnium viribus composita, qua corpusculum quodcunq; trahitur, tendet ad trahentium commune centrum gravitatis, & eadem erit ac si trahentia illa, servato gravitatis centro communi, coirent & in globum formarentur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension of previous result to multiple bodies: the composite attraction on any particle is equivalent to that of a single body formed by coalescing the attracting bodies around their common centre of gravity. Corollary: motion under these attractions proceeds in ellipses about the common centre of gravity if that centre is inertial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XC. Prob. XLIV
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad singula circuli cujuscunq; puncta tendant vires centripetæ decrescentes in quacunq; distantiarum ratione: invenire vim qua corpusculum attrahitur ubivis in recta quæ ad planum circuli per centrum ejus perpendicularis consistit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: compute the force on a point P lying on the axis perpendicular to a circle's plane through its centre A, when each circle point exerts centripetal forces decreasing as any power of distance. Result: the attraction is proportional to the area AHIL (constructed in the proof) divided by AP. Corollaries give explicit reductions: for inverse-square point forces the attraction simplifies to AH/PH; for general power laws the expression involves differences of inverse powers of PA and PH; taking the circle's diameter to infinity yields attraction in a plane proportional to PA^{-(n-2)} when n>1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XCI. Prob. XLV
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire attractionem corpusculi siti in axe solidi, ad cujus puncta singula tendunt vires centripetæ in quacunq; distantiarum ratione decrescentes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a solid symmetric about the axis AB containing a point P on its axis, intersect the solid by circles perpendicular to the axis; apply Prop. XC to each circular section to get an ordinate FK proportional to the attraction of P by that circle; the total attraction is then proportional to the area LABI traced by the curve of FK along the solid. Corollary 1 (cylinder): for a right cylinder and inverse-square point law, the attraction on an axial point P is proportional to AB - PE + PD (i.e., a specific algebraic expression). Corollary 2: formulas for spheroids and segments follow similarly; interior points have attraction proportional to distance from centre under certain conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XCII. Prob. XLVI
rubrics_metrics.description: Dato corpore attractivo, invenire rationem decrementi virium centripetarum in ejus puncta singula tendentium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: construct a sphere or cylinder (or other regular figure) whose pointwise attraction law matches the hypothesized decrement; perform experiments measuring total attraction at various distances; from the observed total attractivity one can infer the pointwise decay law. Thus experimental determination of whole-body attractions determines the law of pointwise decrement required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XCIII. Theor. XLVII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si solidum ex una parte planum, ex reliquis autem partibus infinitum, constet ex particulis æqualibus æqualiter attractivis, quarum vires in recessu a solido decrescunt in ratione potestatis cujusvis distantiarum plusquam quadraticæ, & vi solidi totius corpusculum ad utramvis plani partem constitutum trahatur: dico quod solidi vis illa attractiva, in recessu ab ejus superficie plana, decrescet in ratione potestatis, cujus latus est distantia corpusculi a plano, & Index ternario minor quam Index potestatis distantiarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers a solid whose one face is flat and the rest extends infinitely, composed of equal particles whose pointwise forces decay faster than inverse-square; if the whole solid attracts a particle on both sides of the plane, then at increasing distance from the plane the solid's total attractive force decays as a power of the distance to the plane whose exponent is three less than the exponent of the pointwise distance-law. (Proof begins with geometric decomposition of the solid into many thin planes.)
